Why PCB Tariffs Matter More Than Ever in 2026
For U.S. electronics buyers, tariffs can turn a low unit price into a significantly higher delivered cost. This matters most when sourcing PCBs from China, where Section 301 duties still affect many product categories.
A classification mistake can also slow customs clearance. If your invoice uses the wrong HTS code, omits the Chapter 99 code, or treats a PCBA as a bare PCB, your shipment may face delays, corrections, or unexpected duty bills.
The core question isn't just the board's unit price, but its total landed cost after duty, freight, brokerage, and compliance risk – this is the figure your purchasing team truly needs to compare.
The Right HTS Code: Bare PCBs vs. PCB Assemblies
The first step in calculating PCB import duty from China is identifying exactly what you are importing.
Bare PCBs: HTS 8534.00
Bare printed circuit boards usually fall under HTS 8534.00, which covers printed circuits. A bare board features conductive pathways on an insulating base, devoid of mounted components.
Common examples include:
- Two-layer FR-4 boards
- Four-layer rigid PCBs
- Multilayer bare boards
- Rigid printed circuits without installed components
The normal base duty for many bare PCBs under HTS 8534 is often listed as Free. That does not mean the shipment is tariff-free. If the product has China origin, Section 301 duties may still apply on top of the zero base rate.
PCBAs: HTS 8473.30 and other possible codes

This is the home for the unpopulated PCB as manufactured.
The statistical breakouts within 8534.00.00 distinguish boards primarily by construction. Multilayer boards with three or more layers of conducting material are broken out separately from boards with fewer layers. Boards are also distinguished by substrate: those with a base wholly of impregnated paper (such as common paper-phenolic boards) versus other bases, and a specific line for boards with a ceramic base. Flexible printed circuits (FPCs) have their own breakout. All of these lines are duty-free, so the breakouts matter for statistical reporting rather than duty.
The most important classification point is the boundary between a bare board and a populated assembly. Heading 8534 covers the printed circuit itself. Once components (resistors, capacitors, integrated circuits and the like) are soldered onto the board to create a printed circuit assembly (PCBA), the populated board takes on the character of a part of a finished article and is generally classified as a part of the machine or apparatus it is destined for. For example, a populated board for a computer points toward heading 8473, and a populated board for telecommunications apparatus toward the parts provisions of heading 8517. Which HTS Codes Usually Matter for Bare PCBs and PCBAs?
Bare printed circuits are often reviewed under HTS heading 8534, but a populated assembly may require a different analysis based on what the assembly does. CBP has issued rulings where a bare PCB from China was classified under 8534.00.0040, with the base duty listed as free and an additional China Section 301 duty noted unless excluded. CBP also warns that HTS text and rates can change, so buyers should monitor the current HTS and Chapter 99 treatment.
That example is useful, but it is not a universal answer for every board. A PCB assembly for a medical device, industrial controller, telecom module, or consumer product may be reviewed differently if it has active components and a defined function.

Is there one fixed PCB tariff China 2026 rate?
No. The rate depends on product classification, country of origin, entry date, Chapter 99 treatment, and whether a valid exclusion applies. A bare PCB and a populated PCBA may not be reviewed the same way.
Are bare PCBs from China always classified under HTS 8534?
Many bare printed circuits are reviewed under HTS heading 8534, but final classification depends on the exact product. Use the current USITC HTS and broker or CBP review for the shipment.
Can a PCBA have a different tariff treatment from a bare PCB?
Yes. A populated assembly has components and a function, so the classification discussion may be different from a bare board. Step 6 — Confirm Using Binding Rulings
Many customs authorities offer Binding Tariff Rulings that legally validate classification.
HS Code for PCB Assembly vs Bare PCB vs Electronic Components
A frequent misconception is that PCB, PCBA, and electronic components share the same HS Code. They don’t.
Let’s clear that up.
Bare PCB (HS 8534.00)
A blank printed circuit board without any soldered components.
PCB Assembly (PCBA)
Not covered by 8534 since it includes:
- Microchips
- Resistors
- ICs
- Capacitors
- Connectors
- Solder mask and finishing
These elevate it into categories 8537 or 8543.
Electronic Components (Various Codes)
Individual components (ICs, resistors, LEDs, connectors) fall under entirely different chapters.
This is why misclassification is a top cause of customs delays for electronics manufacturing.
Trade Compliance Requirements for PCB Assembly
Import Duties and Tariffs
Duty rates vary by:
- Country of origin
- Trade agreements
- Level of assembly
- End-use application
PCBA often carries higher tariffs than bare PCBs because it represents higher value and complexity.
Documentation Required for PCB Assembly Shipments
Typical requirements:
- Commercial invoice
- Packing list
- HS code declaration
- Country of origin certificate
- Technical description
- Bill of Materials (if requested)
- ECCN (if applicable for dual-use electronics)
- Compliance certificates (CE, UL, RoHS, ISO, etc.)
Common Misclassification Errors to Avoid
- Using 8534.00 for assembled boards
- Treating complex PCBA as “other electronics” without proper breakdown
- Assuming all assemblies fall under the same subheading
- Not aligning HS Code with end-use device
